subject: Multipath onramp evaluation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN (MercuryBank)

Subject: Multipath onramp assessment request

Hi Rachel —

Thanks for taking a look. We're kicking off a pilot to connect our PCI-scoped inference workloads to Redwood Private. Our security team asked us to evaluate three connectivity patterns: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site (S2S) VPN with BGP.

Attached is a short worksheet with our constraints (latency targets, egress controls, source-IP visibility requirement for logging, and NAT/NAT64 avoidance). High level asks:
- Recommend the least operationally disruptive option for our multi-AZ deployment
- Detailed failure/fallback behaviors (how Redwood would degrade if a path fails)
- Any IP or CIDR limits we should be aware of (peering route limit, ENI scale, etc.)

Can you propose a recommended path and an MOP for a 2-week pilot? Also whether we should expect any additional costs (e.g., interface endpoint data fees, cross-account peering egress).

Thanks — happy to sync with Carlos and the infra team later this week.

—Anita
Ops Manager, MercuryBank

Hi Anita / Carlos —

Thanks for the worksheet — that's helpful. I've looped in Ben from solutions engineering and Kim from account to make sure we cover tech tradeoffs and commercial impacts. High-level summary and next steps below; I'll follow up with a short decision matrix and MOP draft by end of day tomorrow.

Quick summary (short):
- VPC peering: lowest per-packet overhead, predictable latency, but cross-account peering has route table limits and no native private endpoint surface for IP-based allowlisting. Works well if you can accept peering-style CIDR planning.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): best for per-service isolation and source-IP preservation (with our proxy NAT options), but adds per-GB interface endpoint data transfer costs and ENI scaling considerations in your consumer VPCs. Good for strict allowlist models and smaller set of service endpoints.
- S2S VPN (BGP): fastest to stand up for proof-of-concept, supports dynamic routing and on-prem connectivity, but variable latency and less predictable throughput for high token rates; requires HA pairs and monitoring for rekey/MTU issues.

Please find a short set of clarifying questions in the attached — answers there will let us size ENIs, pre-warm connection capacity, and recommend fallback policy (e.g., prefer peering, fall back to PrivateLink; or Primary PrivateLink + VPN fallback).

Can we set a 30-minute sync tomorrow 09/04 at 9:30am PT? If so I'll bring a proposed matrix and a pilot MOP.

Best,
Rachel Kim

Hi all —

Quick technical notes from SE perspective (calling out things Anita asked about):

1) Latency and jitter
- VPC peering: lowest median p99 for intra-region (we've seen 3–6ms for single AZ-to-AZ within region for our dedicated GPU subnet). No additional data-path hops.
- PrivateLink: adds one ENI hop and our NLB/passthrough; typical +2–5ms compared to peering. Good predictability if you keep connection within region and don't chain cross-region endpoints.
- S2S VPN: variable; depends on vendor appliances and encryption offload. For sustained high-throughput token traffic (100s rps), a VPN appliance can become the bottleneck unless you horizontally scale multiple tunnels and session-affinitize.

2) Source IP visibility and auditability
- If Mercury requires original client source IP for downstream logging, peering preserves it. PrivateLink by default SNATs behind ENIs unless you enable our preserve-src-ip proxy mode (we can configure a passthrough proxy in your account using a dedicated ENI pool) — that has operational implications but is feasible for audits. VPN preserves source IP if routing is configured end-to-end.

3) Operational limits and quotas
- Cross-account peering: AWS route table limits depend on your account (typically 1000 routes default, can request increases). Also CIDR overlap blocks peering.
- PrivateLink: each interface endpoint uses ENIs and private IPs; ENI quota on consumer side matters. Also NLB targets and our backend pool scaling must be considered.
- VPN: concurrent tunnels per VGW / customer gateway can be limited; BGP session churn and MTU mismatches are common P0 issues during cut-over.

4) Failure modes and fallback
- Peering failure limited to routing/owner-initiated deletes; fallback requires pre-provisioned PrivateLink or VPN; route priority can't be dynamic across peering & endpoint — we'd handle fallbacks at the application/SDK level or via a DNS-based failover.
- PrivateLink health: internal AWS NLB health checks to our service; we can advertise multi-endpoint DNS and short TTLs so you can fail over quickly.
- VPN: path degradation detectable at BGP; we recommend BFD + BGP for fast failover and a warm standby tunnel to another transit location.

I'll draft a quick matrix with recommended pilot: start with PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for initial PCI pilot to minimize surface area + allowlistability, and configure a dedicated S2S VPN to act as a warm fallback for bulk throughput testing. If Mercury wants source-IP-first and very low latency, migrate core traffic to peering after CIDR planning.

Questions for Mercury (short):
- How many client subnets (CIDR blocks) will connect?
- Expected sustained RPS and peak per-second token load?
- Do you require dedicated egress IP ranges for third-party allowlisting?

—Ben
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Hi Anita —

A couple of commercial/ops notes to include in the MOP and pilot SOW:
- PrivateLink data transfer fees (AWS interface endpoint charges + cross-AZ data fees) will show up on your AWS bill; Redwood can estimate egress if you share expected GB/month.
- For peering, there are usually no per-GB interface charges, but cross-AZ or cross-region traffic will be billed per cloud provider rules — we can model costs vs expected token volume.
- VPN appliances: if Mercury will provide your own edge appliances, please confirm HA/throughput specs; otherwise we can recommend partners (list attached).

Operational asks we need from Mercury to scope Dedicated pre-warm or instance sizing:
- Expected sustained concurrency (sessions) and RPS by endpoint
- Runbooks for incident escalation (who's primary on-call for BGP / rekey events)

If the pilot needs contractual language for a temporary SLA window (e.g., 30-day pilot uptime objective), let me know and I'll raise with legal.

Thanks — Kim
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Hi team —

From a security/compliance lens (PCI constraints), two must-haves for the pilot:
1) Auditable source IPs for all requests touching cardholder data (if you cannot accept SNAT, we will implement our preserve-src-ip passthrough in your VPC with a small managed proxy fleet; requires ENI reservation and extra monitoring).
2) Proof of encryption in transit: for PrivateLink and peering both support TLS; for VPN ensure we document the cipher suites and IKE profiles — we will request telemetry collection for tunnel rekey events.

Action items for Mercury: send the exact list of CIDR blocks and the compliance roster (contacts for PCI attestation). Redwood will provide a short checklist for the pilot (endpoint ACLs, CloudTrail/Syslog requirements, and expected TTLs for DNS failover).

Proposed pilot topology (recommended):
- Primary: PrivateLink interface endpoints scoped to the minimal set of Redwood services required for inference + dedicated ENI pool in consumer VPCs (preserve-src-ip mode enabled).
- Warm fallback: Two S2S VPN tunnels (different providers/exit points) with BGP and BFD for failover testing.
- Goal: Observe latency and throughput for one week, then evaluate migrating critical low-latency flows to peering if route planning permits.

I'll send the compliance checklist and our small MOP fragment (what telemetry we need, what to monitor) as a follow-up.

—Irene
Security & Compliance | Redwood Inference
